conrad-tomlin-minecraft-cvs.title: In a World Without Scarcity, Mike Tomlin Built a CVS
conrad-tomlin-minecraft-cvs.dek: An architectural tour of a civilization where anything is possible and the pharmacy is conveniently located.
conrad-tomlin-minecraft-cvs.author: sorrell
conrad-tomlin-minecraft-cvs.imageAlt: Mike Tomlin explains his Minecraft city during a video tour, appearing beside a view of its waterfront buildings.

imageCredit.label: Mike Tomlin / YouTube, via Steelers Depot

body: For twelve years, Mike Tomlin was building another city. He did this while coaching the Pittsburgh Steelers, which meant spending his working hours being held responsible for decisions made by very large men who remained legally entitled to make their own. Somewhere in the intervals, he went home and worked on a place where a thing stayed exactly where he put it.

The city exists in Minecraft, where Tomlin has recently begun offering walking tours of his municipal holdings. Players arrived and departed while he worked on them. His children grew older. Football seasons ended in the usual combination of explanations and accusations. Somewhere, a hotel needed finishing.

We are accustomed to hearing that coaches live and breathe football, a condition generally presented as admirable rather than something for which the family should arrange an intervention. Every available hour is supposed to disappear into preparation. If a coach admits to a second interest, someone will eventually identify a third-down conversion rate that might have improved had he loved his family less.
Tomlin, it turns out, had been attending to urban development.

We have all come home from work wishing fewer people had been involved in it. After nineteen seasons managing an NFL team, the appeal of a world with substantially fewer independent wills seems fairly accessible. You can explain an assignment to a person perfectly and still watch him do something else. A block offers a different professional relationship.

What makes the city worth examining is what Tomlin did with that authority. He built hotels and luxury residences, a baseball stadium and a soccer stadium, a bank and a pharmacy. The landscape gathers around a body of water. There are rooftops to visit, rooms to inspect, views somebody has considered. He appears to have given considerable thought to what it would be like to spend time there.

I had expected, perhaps unfairly, more conquest. Give an American football coach unlimited resources and I anticipate a fortress, an enormous weight room, possibly a mountain carved into the face of a respected defensive coordinator. Tomlin has a boutique hotel with a spa and a ballroom. His private civilization is prepared to accommodate your wedding.
This raises a more interesting question than whether the coach was wasting time. Why, after a working life organized around competition, does his imaginary world seem so concerned with hospitality?

He knows hotels. He knows the particular version of a city available to a professional football team: the arrival, the meeting room, the room upstairs, the appointed hour downstairs. He has spent years inside buildings intended to make complicated human movements proceed without incident. There is a whole American landscape designed to receive successful men, feed them predictably and put them within reasonable driving distance of their obligations.
Tomlin has built enough of it to suggest that some of those places stayed with him.

body.html: I began to wonder whether he had been collecting improvements. A room with a better view. A more agreeable roof. Lighting that didn’t make everyone look as though they had just received preliminary legal advice. Twelve years is ample time to encounter a hotel lobby and think, with the quiet conviction of a man who has somewhere else to put it, I can do better than this.

body: His attention to lighting is particularly persuasive. You can impose a building on a landscape fairly quickly when materials are unlimited. Making a room feel right requires you to stand in it for a while. It requires a kind of attention that produces very little anyone can measure. Nobody is going to ask how the lamps performed in December.

Naturally, I was suspicious of all this comfort. The luxury residences suggested that even a world without material scarcity had managed to develop a desirable end of town. There was a PNC Bank. Building materials could be summoned at will, yet someone had reserved premises for an institution whose business includes deciding whether you can afford a kitchen.
The CVS completed the neighborhood. A resident could descend from a penthouse containing anything the human mind could conceive and go downstairs for things he had forgotten to pack.

Tomlin’s city carried pieces of the world he knew into the world he controlled. Even the Trump Tower had brought its baggage: during the tour, he clarified that the building predated the first Trump presidency and should not be treated as an endorsement. He had invented an entire municipality and still found himself explaining the context of a decision.

There is an easy argument available here about the limits of American imagination. We give a man freedom from economics and he reproduces expensive housing, commercial banking and convenient access to mouthwash. I could develop that argument at considerable length. I had mentally set aside a paragraph for luxury’s dependence on exclusion.
Then he showed us the aquarium.

It extends through multiple rooms of a residence. Someone had to conceive of that, build around it, return to it and decide whether the fish were contributing adequately to the experience of being indoors. Tomlin was plainly pleased with it. I could find no useful public-policy objection to his pleasure.
This was inconvenient. I had been treating the city as evidence, and its creator appeared to have been treating it as something he liked.

The distinction becomes harder to ignore when you remember how it began. His children were playing Minecraft. He wanted to understand what held their attention, so he joined them. Over time, they moved on and he kept building. They helped preserve the city across successive PlayStations because he needed their technical assistance.

There is a whole family history tucked into that arrangement. The children introduce their father to a place, grow older, and periodically help him keep it. He continues making additions. A game they once played becomes something they make sure he doesn’t lose.

I cannot know what Tomlin was thinking about while he worked on any particular building. I would distrust anyone who claimed to read a playoff defeat in the placement of a staircase. But I find it moving that the project lasted long enough to become a constant while the circumstances around it changed. A season ends. A roster turns over. You still have a room you were meaning to finish.

For years, he could finish that room without us. He could decide the lighting was right without appearing before anyone on Monday to defend it. If something disappointed him, he could change it. If he liked it, that was sufficient reason to leave it alone. These are modest freedoms until you consider how much of his professional life was conducted without them.

I had mistaken complete control for an appetite for domination. Looking at what he made, I find myself considering a less impressive possibility: perhaps he wanted things to work. Perhaps he wanted somewhere pleasant to walk around, where the view was good and the small inconveniences could be corrected by the person who noticed them.

I still think the CVS is funny. I intend to continue thinking so. But an ordinary afternoon, with the necessities close by and nobody demanding an explanation, may be an ambitious enough fantasy for a man who spent nineteen seasons coaching professional football.
He has made something patient and unnecessary. I respect that more than I respect most things currently being described as visionary.

I would like to visit his city. I would like a room overlooking the water, a look at the aquarium, and no scheduled activities before lunch. At some point I would discover that I had forgotten my toothbrush.
The bastard has thought of everything.
conrad-tomlin-minecraft-cvs.receipt: Twelve years of construction. The pharmacy is conveniently located.

marnie-corgi-he-wanted-them-to-know.title: He Wanted Them to Know He Knew.
marnie-corgi-he-wanted-them-to-know.dek: Winning the corgi race was insufficient. He needed witnesses.
marnie-corgi-he-wanted-them-to-know.author: kells
body: There is a photograph from the Seahawks’ corgi race that should be hung in every youth sports facility in America, then covered with a sheet whenever the children arrive.

In it, a corgi in navy has established enough separation from his competitors to turn his head and look back. Behind him, two other dogs are still engaged in the original activity: running as fast as their little legs will carry them. They have dressed for the occasion. They are making an effort. Somewhere nearby, people who love them are presumably saying their names.
The dog in front has decided to check on all that.

You can forgive speed. Some dogs are fast. You cannot account for every variable in a field of animals whose preparation may include eating a receipt. What requires explanation is the discretionary use of the neck. Every fraction of a second spent looking backward is a fraction of a second this animal believes he can afford. He has reviewed the competition and incorporated sightseeing into his race plan.

There is a Usain Bolt quality to the image, except Bolt had the decency to possess legs. This is a throw pillow with access to a higher gear. His undercarriage is practically brushing the venue, and he has still found time to turn around like a man who has just said something unforgivable at a dinner party and wants to see whether it landed.

body.html: We have spent too long assuming that being shaped like this precludes malice. Put a corgi in a little jersey and people immediately begin speaking in a voice they would be embarrassed to have played back in court. Who’s a little athlete? Who’s a speedy boy? Meanwhile, the speedy boy is managing the psychological decline of two colleagues on an NFL field.

body: Consider the social contract under which the other dogs entered this event. A car ride. Some excitement. A brief athletic obligation, followed by extravagant praise. Nobody explained that they might become supporting characters in another corgi’s Jordan documentary. Their owners signed up for enrichment. They are leaving with film to study.
And now they have to go home together.

That is the part the highlight economy never considers. The losing corgi still has to sit in the back seat while someone up front says, “You did so good,” with the strained brightness of a parent leaving a disastrous school production. The dog does not know what a participation trophy is, but he knows the car is quieter than it was on the way there. At a red light, his owner watches the clip again.

The winner, meanwhile, will be impossible at the dog park. You cannot return an animal to ordinary society after he has discovered that his physical gifts come with a broadcast angle. A tennis ball will no longer be enough. He will need the tennis ball thrown in front of people whose opinion matters to him. Fetch will require a media availability.

Naturally, there are questions about the program. Everyone else appears to have brought a pet. Somebody brought a system. I am not accusing this dog of anything, but I would like to understand his relationship with the person who measures his food. We are being asked to accept that this level of separation is available through ordinary kibble and a supportive home environment, and I think the sport deserves a more rigorous conversation.

Still, the legs are only part of the story. The photograph is worth keeping because it catches the moment a wholesome halftime diversion acquires an author. Until that glance, the trailing dogs are simply losing a race. Once he looks back, he is watching them lose it.

Print it wide. Keep the other two in the frame. The empty turf between them is essential to the composition, as is the terrible sincerity of their pursuit. They are still giving everything. He has enough left over to take an interest.
Tonight, all three will be told they are good boys. Two will need to hear it.

marnie-tee-higgins-ankles.title: Tee Higgins’ Ankles Have Asked to Be Buried Separately
marnie-tee-higgins-ankles.dek: The family is contesting Travis Hunter’s appointment as executor.
marnie-tee-higgins-ankles.author: kells
body: Tee Higgins’ upper and lower body have retained separate counsel following Sunday’s encounter with Travis Hunter, ending a partnership that had carried the Cincinnati receiver through childhood, college and several productive NFL seasons. Sources familiar with the separation describe it as sudden, public and geographically complicated.

The dispute began after Hunter intercepted a Joe Burrow pass and encountered Higgins on the return. Higgins attempted to intervene. Hunter presented him with a direction of travel, received his written commitment, then introduced a second direction that had not appeared in any of the preliminary materials.
Higgins’ knees immediately referred the matter to his hips, which were already outside their jurisdiction.

By the time the receiver reached the turf, a small probate office had opened at the spot of the incident. A woman named Doreen was arranging pamphlets. Nobody knows how she got credentialed. She had brought her own laminator and appeared to have been expecting him.

An NFL official subsequently announced that roughing the passer had nullified the interception, creating a difficult theological question: can a man be welcomed into the next life during a play that officially did not occur? The league’s competition committee has referred the matter to the Catholic Church, which requested the broadcast angle and then, in a regrettable breach of protocol, the slow motion.

Higgins, who remains medically alive, has complicated the proceedings by continuing to play football. He finished with 11 catches for 157 yards, repeatedly interrupting preparations for his own memorial. At one point, a funeral director had to move a tasteful arrangement of lilies so Cincinnati could resume its drive.
This has been difficult for the mourners. Every time they begin to find closure, Tee catches another fucking pass.

Hunter has offered to serve as a pallbearer, an overture the family considers both gracious and a threat. Their concern is that he will take one step toward the hearse, cut back across the cemetery and force six grieving men to undergo the same experience. The funeral home’s insurance carrier has requested that he remain seated.

Meanwhile, Higgins’ ankles have declined a joint burial. The left cites irreconcilable differences. The right has relocated to an undisclosed address and is communicating through a cousin. Both dispute the brain’s account that they were adequately prepared for what was coming.

The Bengals maintain that the penalty should settle the matter. Their legal department has submitted the official play-by-play as proof that Hunter never possessed the ball, leaving open the possibility that Higgins simply did that in the presence of a stranger.
Counsel has since withdrawn this argument.

A private viewing will be held Monday, followed by approximately nine million public viewings throughout the week. Guests are asked to silence their phones, although this will make little difference because someone has already projected the clip onto the ceiling of the chapel.
Higgins is expected to attend. There is considerable anxiety about where to seat him.

conrad-deshaun-watson-cleveland-hope.title: Groper Cleveland Is 3–1
conrad-deshaun-watson-cleveland-hope.dek: The Browns finally have something resembling hope at quarterback. For their fans, that creates a much harder question than whether the team can win.

body.html: Cleveland won a football game Thursday night in almost exactly the way Cleveland has spent thirty years insisting it wanted to win football games.
At home. Against Pittsburgh. Under the lights. With the division suddenly looking negotiable.

Deshaun Watson completed 24 of 33 passes for 268 yards and a touchdown, survived an interception and a pair of fumbles, and then took the Browns far enough on their final possession for Andre Szmyt to hit a 56-yard field goal with ten seconds remaining. Cleveland beat Pittsburgh 27–24, moved to 3–1 and won its third consecutive game for the first time since 2021.
This should feel like vindication.
Instead it feels like discovering the cure to a hereditary disease in the glove compartment of a sex pest.

The Browns have spent most of their modern existence searching for the quarterback who could make football in northeastern Ohio feel important again. They drafted Tim Couch first overall and watched him get pulverized behind an expansion roster. They tried Brady Quinn, a handsome Notre Dame quarterback who seemed specifically engineered in a laboratory to make northeastern Ohio believe again. Brandon Weeden was 28 years old when they spent a first-round pick on him, which is a sentence that remains funnier every year. Johnny Manziel arrived with a Heisman Trophy, a money sign and approximately the institutional stability of a nightclub bathroom.
Then they finally drafted Baker Mayfield.

Mayfield won there. He won a playoff game there. Against Pittsburgh, no less. He supplied Cleveland with the first sustained evidence in years that Browns football did not necessarily have to be an elaborate practical joke. Then the organization decided it wanted an upgrade, treated Mayfield like an embarrassing starter marriage, and eventually watched him reconstruct his career somewhere else.
Ruined some. Were ruined by others. Occasionally managed both at once.
And then came Deshaun Watson.
The Browns did not merely acquire a quarterback with “baggage.” Baggage is what television analysts say when a guy yelled at a coordinator or got arrested for something stupid in college.

Twenty-seven women filed civil lawsuits accusing Watson of sexual misconduct during massage appointments. Most cases were settled, and the final two were dismissed in February 2026. Watson has consistently denied wrongdoing, and two Texas grand juries declined to indict him. Separately, the NFL disciplinary process resulted in an 11-game suspension, a $5 million fine and mandatory evaluation and counseling.
Cleveland knew what it was buying.

This was not merely a football team accepting ethical risk in pursuit of competitive advantage. This was a franchise hauling its dignity into a pawn shop, dropping it on the counter and asking how much quarterback play it could get in return.
The answer was supposed to be $230 million worth.
Instead, for years, the Browns received something almost spiritually perfect: bad football.

And I mean that sincerely. There was a grim coherence to it. Cleveland had undertaken one of the most morally radioactive transactions of the modern NFL era and, in exchange, got injuries, poor quarterback play, salary-cap misery and nationally televised humiliation.
Of course it did.
That is how Browns transactions are supposed to work.

Cleveland has been falling down an open manhole and emerging with a quarterback controversy since the Clinton administration. Watson being both grotesque and ineffective at least preserved the natural order. There was no tension for the fan. The moral judgment and the football judgment reached the same conclusion. You could hate the transaction and then spend Sunday afternoon watching the scoreboard provide supporting documentation.
This summer, even the people who actually have to live with the Browns appeared ready to reject the arrangement.

Watson returned to Cleveland’s home field in August during the preseason and got booed heavily. He completed five of 12 passes against Buffalo for 36 yards — NFL.com’s game recap listed 34 — threw an interception, produced no scoring drives and heard it from the crowd throughout his appearance.
The boos were not some spontaneous mystery.
Two days earlier Watson had been asked what reaction he expected from Browns fans.
“I don’t care,” he said. “I don’t care.”
Then the people whose opinion he did not care about expressed that opinion rather loudly, and suddenly he cared.

After the Buffalo game, Watson called the treatment “disrespectful” and said it felt personal rather than merely related to his performance. He later apologized, saying his emotions had gotten the better of him and acknowledging the fans’ frustration.
It was one of those press-conference sequences that becomes funnier the longer you stare at it.

A quarterback whose organization had guaranteed him generational wealth after dozens of women accused him of sexual misconduct appeared genuinely wounded that the paying customers had failed to provide a sufficiently affirming workplace environment.
That has always been the remarkable thing about Watson’s public posture. He possesses an almost supernatural ability to locate himself at the emotional center of every story.
The fans were angry.
Watson was hurt that they were angry.
The franchise had made the transaction.
Groper Cleveland seemed stunned that Cleveland had retained the receipt.
Then the season started.
And the bastard began winning.

Cleveland beat Tampa Bay after trailing by ten in the second half, with Watson throwing two second-half touchdown passes. A week later against Carolina, he returned from a brief injury late in the fourth quarter and threw the go-ahead touchdown before completing the two-point conversion. Then came Pittsburgh, another late drive and another win.
That is where the whole thing becomes genuinely cruel.

Because Browns fans did not make the Watson trade. They did not guarantee the contract. They did not sit in a conference room and determine that whatever moral cost accompanied the acquisition could be amortized over enough wins.
Jimmy Haslam and the Browns did that.
The fans inherited it.

Sports fandom is a terrible vehicle for moral purity because it usually predates the people who eventually embarrass the uniform. Your father took you to Browns games. Maybe his father took him. You remember Bernie Kosar, the Drive, the Fumble, the move to Baltimore, the expansion team, Tim Couch getting hit until the stadium itself seemed embarrassed, 0–16, the quarterback jersey with all the names, Baker finally beating Pittsburgh in Pittsburgh.
And then an owner makes a decision.
What exactly are you supposed to do with forty years of emotional equity? Transfer it to Cincinnati?

That is the dirty little advantage franchises possess over their customers. Teams know loyalty is sticky. They know people cannot take their childhood with them, so an organization can make an appalling decision and reasonably assume that, come Sunday, most of the same people will still put on the sweatshirt.
The institution spends loyalty it did not earn itself.
Thursday night was the bill coming due in reverse.

Pittsburgh tied the game at 24 with 1:46 remaining, which is approximately where generations of Browns fans have been conditioned to recognize the opening bars of catastrophe. Aaron Rodgers had erased an 11-point fourth-quarter deficit. Cleveland had already coughed away control. The script was familiar enough to recite from memory.
Then Watson came back onto the field and moved the football.
Cleveland crossed midfield. The clock drained. Szmyt came out for a 56-yarder and put it through.
Huntington Bank Field erupted.
And thousands of people were forced into perhaps the most uniquely Cleveland emotional experience ever devised: Oh, fuck. This might actually work.
That is the nightmare.

For years there was no moral complication because morality and football agreed. The Watson trade was ugly, the contract was ugly, and the football was ugly. The Browns had made a disgraceful gamble and appeared to have lost it spectacularly. There was something almost reassuring about the universe maintaining that kind of accounting discipline.
Now the scoreboard has become uncooperative.
And sports culture has a very convenient mechanism for what comes next.
It calls it redemption.

The word will arrive slowly because it always does. First Watson will be “resurgent.” Then he will have “persevered.” There will be references to adversity, which is a wonderfully elastic word because it allows us to describe situations without discussing who created them. If Cleveland keeps winning, somebody will eventually produce a beautifully photographed feature about how Watson learned to block out the noise.
The noise.
You know, the women.
The suspension.
The boos.
The consequences of his own public history.

By late September, the framing had already begun shifting. NFL coverage was asking how Browns fans might receive Watson after his improved performances, effectively turning the crowd’s reaction into the next chapter of his football rehabilitation.
I despise this formulation because winning football games is not a moral appeals process.
Twenty-four completions do not vacate allegations. A fourth-quarter drive does not cross-examine anybody. Beating Pittsburgh does not introduce new evidence about Deshaun Watson the man.
It tells us something about Deshaun Watson the quarterback.
Those are different questions.
Professional sports would very much prefer they were not.

The entire machinery of the industry is extraordinarily good at laundering moral questions through performance. Play badly and every controversy remains attached to your name. Play well enough and eventually the adjectives migrate. “Disgraced” becomes “embattled.” “Embattled” becomes “resurgent.” “Resurgent” becomes “veteran.” Somewhere along the way the noun disappears entirely, and suddenly we are discussing leadership.
None of this means Browns fans are required to be miserable.
That would be another form of absurdity.

They are allowed to enjoy beating Pittsburgh. They are allowed to scream when a 56-yard kick goes through. They are allowed to want Cleveland to win twelve games, host a playoff game and make January unpleasant for everyone else. They are even allowed to acknowledge the obvious possibility now sitting in front of them: Watson may be playing good football again.
Fandom does not require ideological consistency. It barely requires sanity.
What it does not require is amnesia.

Browns fans can want the team to win without agreeing that the organization was right. They can celebrate a touchdown without treating it as testimony about the quarterback who threw it. They can accept joy from a football game while refusing the much larger transaction the franchise would love to complete: turning wins into absolution.
That distinction matters because Cleveland may finally be approaching the most perverse possible outcome.
The trade might work.
Not financially. The accounting will remain grotesque. Not morally. Football has no jurisdiction there.
But competitively?
The Browns are 3–1. Watson has now helped produce consecutive late wins, and Thursday night he looked, for meaningful stretches, like exactly what Cleveland thought it was buying four years ago.
That means the organization may eventually receive the thing it gambled everything to obtain.
A franchise quarterback.
And Browns fans may finally receive the thing they have spent most of their football lives begging the universe to provide.
Hope.
With the invoice still attached.

hollis-jameis-winston-turing-test.title: The Jameis Winston Turing Test
hollis-jameis-winston-turing-test.dek: After a decade of motivational philosophy, recursive metaphors and sentences that sound important without technically containing information, Jameis Winston has become an unexpectedly interesting case study in intelligence.

body.html: Jameis Winston was asked a fairly ordinary question on Sunday morning.
How confident was he, carrying the Giants forward?
“One thing that I do is forgetting those that is behind, and reaching forward to what’s ahead,” he said.
Then he stopped talking.

There is a particular look Winston has after he has finished saying something. His eyes widen slightly. His chin settles. Usually he smiles. Then he looks past the reporter and into a middle distance unavailable to the rest of us.
Somewhere only Jameis can go.

It is an almost perfectly constructed Jameis Winston sentence. There is movement. There is philosophy. There is temporal orientation. There is a past, a future and an implied moral responsibility to travel correctly between them.
There is no answer to the question whatsoever.
This is advanced work.
Most athletes evade questions by saying one game at a time. Jameis has discovered that you can evade the question more elegantly by making the reporter briefly wonder whether time itself is linear.

The draw to Jameis Winston is that his actual personality remains strangely elusive despite a decade spent expressing it at maximum volume. The more evidence he provides, the harder he becomes to explain.
So I went back through the archive.
The easiest reading of Jameis is that he is an incredibly reliable sound-bite factory.
This is inadequate.
Jameis occasionally constructs a sentence that sounds as though it has been translated from English into prophecy and then back into English.
In 2022, playing quarterback for the Saints with multiple back fractures, Winston was asked where he was experiencing pain.
“Just pain,” he said.
A pause.
“It was pain, everywhere.”

A person whose body hurts in many locations has described his body hurting in many locations. And yet pain, everywhere is somehow much funnier and much more complete than any medically useful response could have been.
The reporter asked for geography.
Jameis provided the human condition.
Two years later, before the Browns played the Steelers in a wintry mix, a reporter asked Winston what it would take that night.
Naturally, he arrived at Proverbs 21:31. His expression was completely serious, the answer delivered with the solemnity of a surgeon explaining what happens next:
“The horse is prepared for battle, but victory comes from the Lord.”
Then came the weather question.
The same Lord whose omnipotence would predestine the battle had apparently also blessed Jameis with snow and “true football weather.”
His entire disposition changed. He looked like a mastiff puppy discovering that snow for the first time.
Both Jameises were completely sincere.
The Browns won 24–19.
This did not prove Winston correct. It made disproving him considerably harder.
There is also the earlier theorem:

I’m strong if you strong.
We strong, then.
Winston’s strength depends upon the strength of the group. The group’s strength is confirmed by Winston’s strength. Therefore, we strong.
It is a closed motivational system. No external evidence can penetrate it.
Descartes needed a treatise. Jameis needed seven words.
The archive kept producing these, and eventually I stopped asking whether individual statements made sense. I started asking why they felt like they did.
Any serious scholarship must eventually confront Eat a W.
In 2017, Winston stood before his Tampa Bay teammates and attempted to transform winning from an abstract competitive outcome into something edible. He formed his fingers into a W.
Then he ate it.
The Buccaneers subsequently lost 30–10.

For most public figures, this would become a containment problem. You spend several years declining to discuss it. Your publicist asks podcast hosts not to bring it up. Eventually you describe yourself as young and say you’ve grown.
Jameis took another path.
He expanded the lore.

Years later, Peyton and Eli Manning asked him about the W. Winston did not retreat. He explained that the original technique had been flawed because of his mallet fingers. There was apparently a biomechanically superior method. The fingers should be arranged differently. One should “bite the nub.”
Most people eventually become embarrassed by the thing that made them an internet joke.
Jameis understood everyone was laughing and joined us with profound sincerity, while simultaneously adding it to his expanding portfolio of intellectual property.

This is where the investigation becomes difficult, because embarrassment or even subtle historical revision would tell us something. It would establish that there are two Jameises: the person who performed the act and the later person capable of observing the performance from outside himself.
Instead, the later Jameis walked back into the bit and began renovating.

Eat a W became crab legs became commercials became pregame sermons became ManningCast appearances became whatever increasingly interconnected body of work this is. Somewhere along the way, the Jameis Cinematic Universe had begun expanding around us. Nobody had announced Phase Two.
Then FOX sent him to the World Cup.
This may be the most consequential event in the archive, not because Jameis Winston demonstrated previously undiscovered expertise in international football; in fact, he leaned into the lack of it.

For years, Winston’s mercurial answers had produced a minor cottage industry devoted to interpreting Jameisese—figuring out what exactly had happened between the question entering his head and the answer coming back out.
And then FOX dropped him into a blender, surrounded by people who didn’t share his culture, often didn’t share his language, watching a sport whose nuances he freely admitted he was still learning.
And suddenly Jameis required almost no translation at all.

In Dallas, Winston boarded the Oranje Army bus with Dutch supporters. He marched with them toward the stadium in a sea of orange, microphone in hand, shouting about the Dutch Army as though he’d spent his childhood in Rotterdam.
Then the Netherlands played Japan, and afterward Winston changed constituencies.

Japanese supporters have a longstanding tradition of remaining in the stadium after matches to clean the stands. Winston put on a blue Japan shirt with WINSTON across the back, took a trash bag and joined them, moving through the rows collecting cups and wrappers.
Norwegian supporters taught him the Viking Row. Jameis appeared in a horned helmet and faux-fur wrap and began rowing.
Colombian supporters were dancing before a match in Miami. Jameis acquired a jersey and a wig and entered the dance.

He interviewed the parents of American defender Chris Richards about their son’s journey to the World Cup. It became a genuinely touching conversation about injury, perseverance and allowing a child to follow a dream his parents hadn’t chosen for him.
Then Jameis produced a rubber chicken.
They danced with it.
Before Argentina played Algeria, he arrived with an actual goat named Wesley wearing a Lionel Messi jersey. Jameis Winston had transported livestock to a World Cup match to make a visual pun.
The temptation is to call this performance.
But watch him with the Japanese supporters. Watch him with Richards’s parents. Watch how quickly strangers accept him.

Humor usually travels badly. Celebrity travels strangely. American-football celebrity should travel particularly badly at a tournament where the dominant opinion on which football has earned the unmodified name possesses a massive advantage in legacy and, you know, primary-appendage logic.
Jameis somehow crosses these borders almost frictionlessly.
He doesn’t explain himself.
He arrives as himself.
The environment adapts.
At the surface level, one might be inclined to assume Jameis Winston is trolling all of us.
The theory doesn’t survive much scrutiny.

Trolling requires too much distance. A troll knows where normal behavior is and intentionally steps outside it. The joke depends upon the performer maintaining some private separation between the person doing the ridiculous thing and the person who knows it is ridiculous.
Jameis appears to offer something more interesting.

The question isn’t whether he is performing. All public people perform. The question is whether Jameis Winston has achieved a form of self-awareness so complete that he no longer needs to modify the self being observed.
He knows how to Eat a W. He knows about the memes. He knows television wants Jameis because Jameis may do something television did not anticipate.
And his response to acquiring this information appears to have been:
continue being exactly the same person.
That’s sophisticated.
Perhaps accidentally.
Perhaps not.
Once performance, sincerity and self-awareness become this difficult to separate in a human being, the distinction takes on a whole new pattern of modern significance.
Because machines are trying to cross the same boundary from the opposite direction.

In 1950, Alan Turing proposed what became known as the imitation game. Rather than settle the abstract question of whether a machine could think, he proposed examining whether its responses could become sufficiently human such that an interrogator could no longer reliably distinguish machine from person.

It is a test about intelligence and self-awareness. Underneath it is the public-facing, existential problem: how do we recognize an authentic mind when all we are permitted to observe is its performance?
Recently, an AI-generated Jameis Winston clip circulated online.
The fake Winston purportedly told his Giants teammates that one man with one crab leg was mortal, but 53 men with crab legs become an unstoppable force.
It was fake.
People had to check.
At first this seems like another familiar story about synthetic media. Then you examine the control group.
Eating the letter W via his fingers?
Real.
Returning years later to explain the correct finger mechanics for eating said W?
Real.
Bringing an actual goat dressed as Lionel Messi to the World Cup?
Real.
Revisiting the crab-leg scandal for a DoorDash commercial by performing a reflex challenge with crab legs?
Real.
The machine has a considerable advantage.
Its training data is insane.

This creates what we might come to think of as the Jameis Winston Turing Test: can an artificial intelligence produce a statement attributed to Jameis Winston that is sufficiently strange to seem authentic without becoming so strange that even Jameis Winston would not plausibly have said it?
Perhaps Jameis himself doesn’t particularly care where that boundary is.

Artificial intelligence is forcing us into increasingly complicated arguments about authenticity. If a machine can perfectly imitate your voice, your face, your vocabulary and your mannerisms, what remains that makes the performance you?
We tend to answer with some version of interiority: intent, self-awareness, the private consciousness behind the performance.
Jameis complicates this because the external performance appears almost perfectly resistant to evidence about how that performance is perceived or originated.

The internet tells him he’s ridiculous. Jameis smiles. Television tells him he’s compelling. Jameis smiles. The meme gets repeated back to him. Jameis adds technical detail. A network drops him into an unfamiliar culture on the other side of the sporting world.
Jameis finds a trash bag.
The machine can imitate the output, but I’m not sure it can reproduce whatever internal arrangement makes that response feel inevitable.
Maybe that is the remaining distinction. Not intelligence, language or even originality.
Something irreducible and outside the boundaries of the algorithm: the capacity to remain genuinely unpredictable even after everyone thought they had the pattern.
I went back to the clip that started all of this.
Forgetting those that is behind.
Reaching forward to what’s ahead.
I had laughed the first time. After going through the archive, I watched it again.
Maybe the grammar isn’t the point.
The information definitely isn’t the point.

There is something radical about a person who has been shown, repeatedly and at enormous scale, exactly how the world perceives him and has apparently concluded that the appropriate response is not reinvention but greater fidelity.
That doesn’t make every Jameis sentence profound. Some of them contain absolutely nothing. That’s part of the problem, and part of the charm.
I still don’t know whether Jameis Winston knows exactly what he’s doing. I’m increasingly convinced that’s the wrong question.

He knows we’re watching. He knows why we’re watching. And somehow that knowledge has not made him more guarded, more calculated or less strange. More remarkably, it hasn’t made him predictable or tempted him into simply overplaying Jameis Winston for an audience.
Shakespeare had all the world as a stage. Jameis fired the editor.
Maybe that’s the test.
Maybe that’s the part the machine still can’t do.
The clip ends with Jameis gazing again into that truly unknowable middle distance.
For one brief moment, you can’t tell whether he’s just said something incredibly profound or absolutely nothing at all.
Then he smiles.

dashiell-jaguars-london-future.title: Is the NFL’s Future Hiding Inside Its Weirdest Franchise?
dashiell-jaguars-london-future.dek: The Jacksonville Jaguars spent years looking like an NFL problem to be solved. In London, they may have accidentally become something else.
dashiell-jaguars-london-future.author: pike
dashiell-jaguars-london-future.imageAlt: NFL fans gathered in London for an international game.
body: There are easier ways to build a global sports franchise.
You can begin in London, for instance.

You can be founded in 1882 by schoolboys from a cricket club, play your first matches on the Tottenham Marshes, spend the next 144 years accumulating trophies, enemies, songs, grievances and several generations of people who believe allegiance to you is less a consumer preference than an inherited medical condition.
Or you can begin in Jacksonville in 1993.

The National Football League awarded the city an expansion franchise on November 30 of that year. Twenty-one months later, the Jaguars played their first regular-season game. They had no ancestors to honor, no ancient ground to mourn, no grandfather who could explain what the club meant before television ruined it.
They had to make the rest themselves.

There were the unexpectedly excellent Mark Brunell teams, which reached two AFC Championship Games before the franchise was six years old. There was Fred Taylor. Maurice Jones-Drew. The stadium pools. Blake Bortles and the strange civic confidence required to believe in him.

Gardner Minshew arrived in aviators, a headband and a mustache that looked inherited from a regional contractor. Jacksonville did not merely tolerate him. It adopted him almost immediately. Minshew Mania became one of those rare sports phenomena that made perfect sense only after it happened: an overlooked sixth-round quarterback becoming a genuine folk hero for a young franchise still deciding what its folklore should look like.
The Jaguars have made history. They have simply had to make it faster and in stranger ways than everybody else.

body.text: Then there is London.

body: The Jaguars began playing an annual home game at Wembley in 2013. At first the arrangement carried the unmistakable smell of contingency. Jacksonville was one of the NFL’s smallest markets. London was the enormous foreign city the league had spent years staring at. The Jaguars were young, commercially ambitious and available.
The conclusion assembled itself.
Surely, they were leaving.
That conclusion has now survived long enough to become almost quaint.

The Jaguars have played 14 regular-season games in London since 2013. Eleven came at Wembley, three at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. This season they will play two designated home games there on consecutive Sundays, first against Philadelphia at Tottenham on October 11 and then against Houston at Wembley on October 18. It is the third time the franchise has played back-to-back games in Britain.
There was a time when any one of those sentences would have generated another week of relocation stories.
Now it mostly generates travel information.
That may be the first strange thing worth noticing.
The second is that Jacksonville, after years of being treated as temporary, has committed itself rather aggressively to staying put.

The city and franchise are in the middle of a $1.4 billion stadium redevelopment backed by a 30-year lease and non-relocation agreement. Construction has reduced capacity this season to roughly 42,500, and the team will temporarily move its 2027 home schedule to Orlando before returning to the rebuilt stadium in 2028.
This is an unusual way to leave a city.
Shad Khan has spent years insisting he does not intend to.
In 2018 he attempted to buy Wembley Stadium, producing precisely the reaction anyone could have anticipated. Jaguars. Wembley. Owner buys stadium. Pack the moving vans.
Khan called Wembley the Jaguars’ “home away from home” and argued that strengthening the team in London would make its future in Jacksonville more secure.
At the time, that sounded like the sort of sentence corporate executives produce when two ideas are being asked to coexist against their natural instincts.
Eight years later, it has become difficult to dismiss.
The Jaguars are more anchored in Jacksonville than they have ever been. They are also more comfortable in London than they have ever been.

This year, because the Jacksonville stadium is operating at reduced capacity, the Jaguars moved forward an international-game obligation originally expected later in the decade. They sacrifice a smaller-capacity Jacksonville date now and recover a full-capacity home game once the new stadium is finished.

A football team has converted geography into inventory. Jacksonville is borrowing a home game from its own future, moving it across the Atlantic, using the absence to accelerate construction in Florida and planning to redeem the asset later in a more valuable building.
They are not merely playing in London anymore.
They are arbitraging it.
Tottenham Hotspur Stadium rises in North London on almost the same patch of earth where the football club began accumulating meaning in the nineteenth century.
Tottenham Hotspur is 144 years old. Its history can be measured in wars, monarchs, economic eras and arguments about Arsenal.
The Jacksonville Jaguars are 31.
Their first season occurred the same year Toy Story was released.
On Sunday, the Jaguars will walk into Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and be treated not as an American exhibition but as a home team.
Tottenham is one of the things old sports institutions aspire to become: inseparable from a place while recognizable nearly everywhere else.
Its stadium sits inside that history but was designed, rather ingeniously, not to be imprisoned by it.

The building has a retractable grass surface. Underneath it sits a separate field specifically for American football. It has NFL-specific locker rooms and media facilities. Tottenham and the NFL have extended their partnership through the 2029-30 season, guaranteeing at least two regular-season NFL games there each year and formally designating the stadium the “Home of the NFL in the UK.”
Daniel Levy has been straightforward about the logic: events create recurring revenue that can be reinvested into the football club.
That is particularly useful during seasons when the football club itself is less cooperative.

Tottenham opened the 2026 Premier League season disastrously. By late September, after an enormous squad rebuild, Spurs were winless, near the bottom of the table and enduring one of their worst starts of the Premier League era.

For the financial year ending June 2025, Tottenham reported £565.3 million in revenue and other income, citing sponsorship, merchandising and stadium events as commercial strengths even as poor football performance hurt media revenue. The club still recorded a £94.7 million after-tax loss.
The easy joke is that the Jaguars have somehow become the more functional football operation in Tottenham.
The better observation is that these organizations arrive at the same building from opposite ends of sporting history.
Tottenham has spent nearly a century and a half accumulating meaning until the club and the place became almost impossible to separate.
Jacksonville has spent three decades accumulating meaning while remaining unusually free to decide what comes next, and where.
That difference matters in London.

London is perhaps the worst possible city in which to argue that place no longer matters in sports. Its clubs carry neighborhoods in their names. Their rivalries are mapped onto rail lines, boroughs and old class boundaries. Supporters inherit allegiance in ways American franchises tend to describe aspirationally in marketing decks.
Into that environment comes Jacksonville: young, improvised, faintly renegade, successful enough to be taken seriously and still new enough to behave as though some of the old rules are negotiable.
England arrives as the old power: storied, established, heavy with accumulated prestige, and currently watching one of its great football institutions stumble through a miserable period.
Jacksonville arrives as the upstart: younger, less polished, less encumbered by tradition, and discovering that the lack of an old order can sometimes be its own advantage.
The colonies, after all, did not defeat Britain by possessing more history.
They had considerably less of it.

Tottenham’s identity is inherited. Jacksonville’s has been assembled in public, often awkwardly, sometimes brilliantly, from pieces that would have looked ridiculous in advance: Minshew Mania, pools in a football stadium, annual trips to Wembley, an owner who once tried to buy England’s national stadium.
Those things are not substitutes for history anymore.
They are Jaguars history.
And London has become part of it.
That is what makes the old relocation conversation increasingly unsatisfying.
For years the question was simple: Jacksonville or London? Florida or England? Stay or move?
But the Jaguars have spent more than a decade demonstrating that those choices may not be as mutually exclusive as everyone assumed.
Tottenham still makes the strongest possible case for the traditional model. Its value is bound up in the fact that Tottenham Hotspur could not plausibly become Tottenham Hotspur somewhere else.
Jacksonville is testing something much looser.
Not because Jacksonville means nothing. It clearly does not. There are now adults who grew up with the team, families whose Jaguars history spans generations, and a city investing heavily to keep it.
But thirty-one years is young enough that the franchise can still add geography without necessarily surrendering identity.
Pittsburgh could play an annual game in London. It would be difficult to make London part of what the Steelers are.
Green Bay could sell out Wembley tomorrow. Nobody would mistake Wembley for part of the Packers’ institutional geography.
The Jaguars have already crossed some quieter threshold.
London is no longer simply where Jacksonville plays sometimes.
It has become one of the places where Jacksonville happened.

That may remain unique to them. The peculiar combination of Khan, a young franchise, small-market economics, repeated games and more than a decade of institutional repetition may prove impossible to reproduce.
Or it may be exactly why the Jaguars matter.

The NFL has nine international games on the 2026 schedule across four continents, seven countries and eight stadiums. Teams hold international marketing rights. Fans follow franchises they may never see in their home cities. Stadiums increasingly operate as entertainment infrastructure with football attached rather than monuments devoted exclusively to one tenant.

Jacksonville did not arrive here through some immaculate master plan. Revenue pressures, league ambition, Khan’s appetite for London and the franchise’s own willingness to experiment all pushed in the same direction. What began as an accommodation kept being renewed until it developed traditions, constituencies and commercial logic of its own.

British Jaguars supporters came back. London stopped feeling temporary. The league built another stadium relationship. The annual oddity became part of the calendar. Eventually the arrangement became useful enough that Jacksonville could move a future game across an ocean because its stadium math worked better that way.
London now feels less like an exception the NFL tolerates and more like a piece of the schedule the league has learned to depend on.
Sunday offers a particularly elegant picture of what followed.

The stadium itself carries 144 years of inherited sporting memory. Into it walks a franchise with barely three decades of self-invented mythology, much of it assembled from unlikely quarterbacks, improbable playoff runs, London Sundays and decisions nobody else in the league quite had reason to make.
Tottenham demonstrates the almost incalculable value of belonging unmistakably to one place.
Jacksonville raises a different question:
What happens when belonging to one place no longer requires belonging only to it?
Perhaps the Jaguars remain a wonderful outlier — a peculiar franchise, an unusually international owner and a relationship with London that no other NFL organization can reproduce.
Or perhaps everyone has spent thirteen years looking at the league’s strangest franchise and mistaking a prototype for a punchline.
The Jaguars probably aren't moving to London.
A decade from now, that may sound like an oddly twentieth-century way of describing what happened.

hollis-west-virginia-medical-assistance.title: West Virginia's Medical Assistance Raises Some Questions
hollis-west-virginia-medical-assistance.dek: Cincinnati's Medical Emergency Acquired a Second Medical Emergency
hollis-west-virginia-medical-assistance.author: crane

imageCredit.label: TNT Sports broadcast / X via The Spun

hollis-west-virginia-medical-assistance.imageAlt: Cincinnati defensive lineman Josh Hough transported by a medical cart at West Virginia.
body: There is a basic understanding in organized football that when a player gets injured, the people responsible for removing him from the field will make some effort to improve his condition.
On Saturday in Morgantown, that understanding was subjected to an unexpected field test.

Cincinnati defensive lineman Josh Hough suffered a lower-body injury against West Virginia. Medical personnel loaded him onto a cart for transport to the locker room, where he could receive further treatment.
Then the cart backed into a wall.
Not near a wall. Not toward a wall. Into the wall, with Hough's already injured leg extended from the vehicle.
The collision appeared to press his foot against the stadium infrastructure, producing the sort of reaction generally associated with the original injury rather than the medical response.
The driver, whose West Virginia shirt suggested at least some familiarity with the home team's interests, had apparently failed to account for the wall.
The wall was not moving. West Virginia had enjoyed considerable advance notice of its location. It had been standing there throughout the afternoon, performing its responsibilities without incident.
Hough was ruled out for the remainder of the game. Whether the collision aggravated his injury remains unclear.

College football has invested extraordinary resources in player safety. Saturday's incident suggests at least one remaining vulnerability in the system. Maybe we should consider not backing the injured player into the building.
In the interests of competitive integrity, perhaps Cincinnati should handle its own transportation next time.

conrad-allow-me-to-reintroduce-myself.title: Allow Me to Reintroduce Myself
conrad-allow-me-to-reintroduce-myself.dek: Finding someone equal to the occasion is easier when you consider yourself the occasion.
conrad-allow-me-to-reintroduce-myself.author: sorrell
conrad-allow-me-to-reintroduce-myself.imageAlt: Jay-Z at the Shawn Carter Foundation Carnival in 2011.

body.html: According to Dave Brooks’s reporting in Puck, the search for the next Super Bowl halftime performer has reached a decision. Miley Cyrus and Justin Bieber were among the artists considered. Jay-Z, whose Roc Nation advises the NFL on the selection, reportedly had someone else in mind. The booking remains unconfirmed.

body: Consider the possibilities. A changing audience. A new generation of fans. An opportunity to put something progressive, energizing and unexpected on one of the world’s biggest stages. An entire industry of performers, any one of whom might turn those few minutes into the defining appearance of a career.
Who could meet that moment? Who could carry the culture forward? Who could make people look up from their phones and feel they were witnessing something they hadn’t already seen?
Take your time, Jay. Look everywhere.

Consider the reach. The catalogue. The sheer presence. Someone who could command that stage without being swallowed by it. Someone whose contribution to music you might, if pressed, describe as historic.

And then there is the question of trust. You need an artist whose judgment you respect. Whose vision you understand. Someone you can recommend without reservation, knowing they will appreciate the magnitude of the opportunity.
After considering what the world needed to hear, Jay-Z had a name.
Jay-Z.

The man will be fifty-seven by kickoff. There is nothing inherently wrong with a fifty-seven-year-old performing at the Super Bowl. There is something magnificent about searching for the future of entertainment and finding a man who happens to use the same toothbrush as you. Quite the contribution to the distinguished internet tradition of being deeply moved by your own selection.

body.alt: Edited internet meme depicting Barack Obama awarding a medal to himself.

body: And yes, he has the songs. Of course he has the fucking songs. That is what makes this such a luxurious act of self-indulgence. He can reportedly give himself the biggest booking in music and make anyone questioning the arrangement sound as though they’ve never heard The Blueprint. We have heard it, Jay. We would also have enjoyed hearing you tell yourself no.

Nobody is asking him to develop an inferiority complex. The man has earned the right to think highly of his work. But there is a considerable distance between believing you belong on that stage and being involved in choosing who gets it, then deciding the audience has waited long enough for you.

Imagine being another artist and learning that you lost out to Jay-Z. Perfectly respectable. Then imagine learning that the man who helped decide this was also Jay-Z. You could ask for feedback, although presumably it would be that you should have been Jay-Z.

The show could be excellent. The opening bars could do exactly what opening bars are supposed to do. People could leap off sofas. The catalogue could justify every minute. By Monday, anyone still discussing how he got the booking would be accused of refusing to enjoy themselves.

And there he would be, vindicated twice: once as the performer, once as the visionary who recognized his potential. A standing ovation for the artist would double as an outstanding performance review for the man involved in selecting him. Even the applause would be working two jobs for Jay-Z.

This is what makes the prospect so exquisitely irritating. We could enjoy every minute and still have watched a man interpret an enormous opportunity to look outward as a request to take stock of his own achievements. The world is changing. The audience is changing. Somewhere in all that movement, Jay-Z has reportedly located the urgent need for more Jay-Z.

By the final song, with the crowd singing along, he could almost make choosing himself look generous. All these people, having this wonderful time. All this happiness he would have denied them by exercising a little restraint.
He could have given the stage to somebody else. Just imagine how selfish that would have been.
